crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Satellite Imagery
children.blurb: Satellite imagery as alternative data refers to the use of overhead optical, radar, and multispectral images to measure economic activity that is not captured in standard financial statements or government releases.

children.name: Card Transaction Data
children.blurb: Card transaction data refers to aggregated and anonymized records of purchases made with credit, debit, and prepaid cards, used by economists and analysts to track consumer spending, revenue trends, and regional economic activity.

children.name: Sensor and Shipping Data
children.blurb: Sensor and shipping data as alternative data covers physical-world signals from vessel transponders, port sensors, weather stations and cargo telemetry, used to estimate trade flows, commodity supply, congestion and industrial activity.

children.name: Mobile Location Data
children.blurb: Mobile location data refers to aggregated or individual-level geospatial records collected from smartphones and other connected devices, used as an alternative dataset for economic analysis, retail footfall, mobility, and real estate.

children.name: Web Data Collection
children.blurb: Web data collection in alternative data means gathering publicly available information from websites, forums, job boards, app stores, social media, and regulatory filings to build datasets that supplement traditional financial and economic data.

sections.body: Alternative data means using information that does not come from standard financial statements or government statistics. Artificial intelligence is actually reading satellite photos to count cars in retail parking lots, estimate crop conditions, and measure oil held in storage tanks. Card transaction data is aggregated and anonymized to track spending by category, region, and merchant type. Sensor and shipping data from vessel transponders, truck GPS units, and port equipment feeds models of supply chain movement and delay. Mobile location data measures foot traffic to stores, offices, and transit stations. Web data collection scrapes job postings, product prices, and public reviews to build real time economic indicators.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven across these sources. Satellite imagery analysis is dependable for physical counts like ships at berth or cars in lots, but it struggles with subtle signals such as consumer sentiment or service output. Card transaction data is widely used and timely, yet it misses cash payments and some bank transfers, so it overrepresents card heavy households. Sensor and shipping data is good at detecting current congestion and delays, but it cannot reliably predict demand shocks or future trade volumes. Mobile location data is noisy and privacy constrained, with opt in panels that may not match the general population. Web data collection is cheap and fast but often unstructured, requiring heavy cleaning and breaking when websites change their layouts. Honest limits include stale or biased samples, uneven geographic coverage, and unresolved legal questions around personal data.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The Satellite Imagery page explains how orbital photos become economic counts, from parking lot occupancy to crop health and oil storage. Card Transaction Data covers what aggregated spending panels can and cannot reveal about consumer behavior. Sensor and Shipping Data walks through vessel transponders, truck GPS, and port sensors as supply chain signals. Mobile Location Data describes how foot traffic panels are built and why their samples are biased. Web Data Collection shows how scraping job boards, price pages, and forums creates alternative indicators. Together these pages move from physical observation to digital exhaust, each with different latency, coverage, and legal risk.
